To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cytoplasmically derived factors can regulate gene expression in mammalian cells.
the albumin gene in rat hepatoma cells is negatively controlled by a cytoplasmically located factor which is short-lived.
the albumin gene is suppressed by a short-lived cytoplasmically localized factor in cytoplasmic hybrids between rat hepatoma and mouse fibroblastic cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of gene expression and regulation in eukaryotes, particularly in somatic cell hybrids.
the identification of cytoplasmic components that regulate gene expression and with the mechanisms by which these components function.
the role of the cell cytoplasm in the control of gene regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cytoplasmic regulator is a protein which is synthesized by the cybrid cells and which is not renewed in the cytoplasm of the cybrid cells in the absence of a nucleus.
the cytoplasmic regulator is a short-lived factor that is not synthesized by the fibroblast and that is required for albumin gene expression.
the cytoplasmic component is a short-lived factor which is responsible for negative control over albumin expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the nucleus is not necessary for albumin production and that a cytoplasm factor is involved in its regulation.
we have shown the existence of a short-lived negative regulator of the rat albumin gene which is present in fibroblasts but not in hepatoma cells.
the nucleus of a differentiated cell can control gene expression in a cytoplasm of a non-differentiated cell, but this effect is short-lived and is dependent on continued nuclear function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cytoplasmic environment is an important regulator of gene expression.
it is possible to study the regulation of gene expression in a system in which the cytoplasm of the cells is modified but the nuclear DNA remains unchanged.

it is possible to prepare hybrid cells which have not undergone extensive chromosomal losses or rearrangements and which are therefore suitable for the study of the role of cytoplasmic control in gene regulation.
